title: About the ancient city of Athens and its surrounding region, Attica
author: Attic Inscriptions Online

title: Tyrants, democrats and the first silver ‘owl’ coins of Athens
author: Gillan Davis, Janne Blichert-Toft, Liesel Gentelli & Francis Albarède
scope: Archaic silver sources; chronology of the Laurion discovery; evidence against a simple one-event origin story.
note: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 17, 122. New analyses of 52 archaic coins plus 12 legacy measurements; the authors’ interpretation is identified as such.

title: The Reminting of Athenian Silver Coinage, 353 B.C.
author: John H. Kroll
scope: Pi-style, folded flans, reminting, and the proposed 353 BCE fiscal context.
note: Hesperia 80(2), 229–259. Consulted in the author’s online copy. Later work revisits the date; this atlas does not treat 353 as settled.

title: Athenian Tetradrachm Coinage of the First Half of the Fourth Century BC
author: John H. Kroll
scope: Early fourth-century profile-eye coinage, surviving hoards, and reminting as an explanation for rarity.
note: Revue belge de Numismatique 157, 3–26. Relative classification is more secure than every absolute date.

title: When is an owl not an owl? An analysis of Attic tetradrachms circulating in the southern Levant in the late fifth and fourth centuries BCE
author: Liesel Gentelli, Gillan Davis, Francis Albarède, Janne Blichert-Toft & Haim Gitler
scope: Three-quarter-eye owls, contested “Eastern imitation” attributions, the 404 BCE endpoint, and revised Pi-style discussion.
note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 70, 105634. Consulted via the author’s full-text copy on ResearchGate. The paper reports 22 sampled coins; the atlas avoids converting a sample-specific argument into a universal authentication rule.

title: Law on approvers (dokimastai) of silver coinage, 375/4 BC (AIO 819 / RO 25)
author: Translation: Stephen Lambert & P. J. Rhodes; Attic Inscriptions Online
scope: Official testing, foreign owl-type silver, and bronze- or lead-cored coins.
note: The restored wording of the foreign-coin clause is uncertain. Its treatment of good foreign silver is not equated here with a blanket legal-tender rule.

title: The circulation and distribution of classical Greek coinage
author: Zane Mullins
scope: Hoard-based distribution of Classical Greek coinages, including Athenian coins in Egypt, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Iran and Afghanistan, and discussion of foreign imitations.
note: The sample covers 550–300 BCE, not every period or every find. Some older hoard descriptions combine Athens and imitations. Hoard locations do not reconstruct exact trade routes; use, issuing intent and movement mechanisms remain interpretive questions.

title: Hoards and Overstrikes: The Numismatic Evidence
author: Margaret Thompson · Penn Museum, Expedition 21(4)
scope: Published hoard evidence for Athenian coins in Sicily, southwest Anatolia, Egypt, the Levant and farther east; discussion of coins used as bullion.
note: A historical synthesis retained for its documented geographic examples. Its chronology and broad attribution arguments are not automatically adopted; later research, including Gentelli et al. (2026), revisits some eastern imitations. This overview is not a complete gazetteer of finds.

title: Mazaces, Babylon · Le Rider 1997 pseudo-atheniens 10
author: IRIS / University of Oxford
scope: An Athena–owl type attributed to Mazaces and the mint of Babylon, in Babylonia.
note: IRIS gives this type a broad 350–300 BCE range. The geographic introduction uses the mint attribution; it does not extend this date range to every Babylonian owl-type coin or imply an exact issue date. No new specimen photograph is embedded.

title: Greek Art: From Prehistoric to Classical — Coins of Ancient Greece
author: Michael Norris · The Metropolitan Museum of Art
scope: “Origin and Technique,” printed p. 55 (PDF page 57): hand-engraved dies, a lower obverse die fixed in an anvil, a metal blank and an upper reverse die struck with a hammer.
note: The site uses an original schematic to explain this general method. It does not reproduce the publication’s artwork or reconstruct a particular Athenian workshop, tool set, strike count or coin specimen.

title: Getting started on ancient Greek: 9.1 Athens
author: The Open University · OpenLearn
scope: Ancient Athenian theta letterforms, including the circle with a central dot.
note: Activity 14 compares dotted and crossed theta on Themistocles ostraka. These are examples of Athenian writing, not a catalogue or dating source for the illustrated coin.

title: Erechtheion building accounts, 408/7 BC (IG I³ 476)
author: Translation: Stephen Lambert & Robin Osborne; Attic Inscriptions Online
scope: Wages and piece-rates on the Erechtheion. AIO's note 6 states that the architect and the labourers, both skilled and unskilled, were employed either on a day-wage of 1 dr. or on piece-rates computed on the basis of that wage.
note: Most surviving entries record piece-rates for named tasks rather than counted days; the 1 dr. day-wage is AIO's editorial summary of the accounts, not a quoted line of the stone. The accounts cover one year of finishing work at one building.

title: The First Athenian Owls: Symbols of What, Exactly?
author: Peter van Alfen · American Numismatic Society, Pocket Change
scope: The civic legibility of the owl type and its longevity: the Athenians saw little need to change the basic design until they ceased minting tetradrachms completely in the first century BC.
note: A curator's public-facing post, not a peer-reviewed article. The Peisistratid branding explanation is reported there as a current explanation rather than asserted. The claim concerns the basic type; style and detail changed considerably.

title: Birds 1106–1108
author: Aristophanes; translation Eugene O'Neill, Jr.; Perseus Digital Library
scope: The bird chorus promises the competition judges that the owls of Laurion will never fail them, that they will move in and nest in the judges' money-bags, and that they will hatch out small change.
note: A comic bribe aimed at the play's judges, not a report of monetary practice. The Greek text is at Perseus text 1999.01.0025, same card; line 1108 reads ἐννεοττεύσουσι κἀκλέψουσι μικρὰ κέρματα. O'Neill's 1938 English may remain in copyright: link and quote briefly rather than reproducing the passage.

title: Silver Tetradrachm, Athens, 515 BCE–482 BCE · 2008.39.34
author: American Numismatic Society
scope: A worn archaic Athenian tetradrachm, 17.047 g, 21 mm, recorded with one chisel cut and a secondary treatment of Cut, from the Asyut hoard (IGCH 1644).
note: The record documents a cut on this specimen. It does not state who made the cut, when or why, and a single record is not evidence for how common test cuts are. Citing it implies no museum endorsement and offers no authentication guidance.

title: The Histories 7.144
author: Herodotus; translation A. D. Godley; Perseus Digital Library
scope: Revenues from the mines at Laurium; a proposed distribution of ten drachmae a man; Themistocles persuading the Athenians to build two hundred ships instead, for the war with Aegina.
note: Herodotus gives no year, names no coin type, and ties the ships to the Aeginetan war rather than to Salamis. Godley's own footnote calculates that ten drachmae a head would be far too small a sum to build two hundred ships and reads the passage as a contribution to a shipbuilding fund.

title: Athenian Constitution 22.7 (Athenaion Politeia)
author: Aristotle; translation H. Rackham; Perseus Digital Library
scope: A hundred-talent profit from the newly discovered mines at Maronea; Themistocles has it lent to the hundred richest Athenians; a hundred triremes are built, and with these the Athenians fight the naval battle at Salamis.
note: This account conflicts with Herodotus 7.144 on the mine, the number of ships and the mechanism. Rackham prints the archon's name as Nicomedes; the archon of 483/2 BC is usually printed Nikodemos. The conventional 483/2 BC date comes from the archon year, not from the text.

title: The ANS's Greatest Coins: the first Athenian “Owl”. The dollar of the ancient Greek world
author: Peter van Alfen · American Numismatic Society, Pocket Change
scope: Record of where the phrase “the dollar of the ancient Greek world” actually comes from: the headline of an ANS video post about the first Athenian owl.
note: Held as evidence about the phrasing, not as support for a claim. The analogy is a headline on a video post and is not argued in the body text. Treat it as popular framing attributable to ANS outreach, never as a research finding.

title: Athenian Constitution 62.2 (Athenaion Politeia)
author: Aristotle; translation H. Rackham; Perseus Digital Library
scope: State pay for public duties: a drachma for an ordinary meeting of the Assembly and a drachma and a half for a sovereign one, half a drachma for the jury-courts, five obols for the Council, and a drachma a day for the archon for Salamis.
note: The Athenaion Politeia describes arrangements of its own time, the later fourth century BC, not a rate fixed for every year. Its authorship is debated; it is transmitted under Aristotle's name. Rackham's 1952 translation may remain in copyright: link rather than reproduce at length.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War 6.31.3
author: Thucydides; translation Richard Crawley; Perseus Digital Library
scope: The Sicilian expedition of 415 BC: the treasury giving a drachma a day to each seaman, with the trierarchs adding bounties on top of the state's pay.
note: A rate for one expedition that Thucydides presents as exceptionally costly, not a standing naval wage. Perseus publishes this translation under CC BY-SA 3.0 US.

title: Cupellation and litharge in their technological context at Laurion, Attika (Greece) – From Prehistoric to Hellenistic and early Roman periods
author: George D. Papadimitriou · Deutsches Bergbau-Museum Bochum, Der Anschnitt Beiheft 50
scope: How Laurion ore became silver: smelting in charcoal-fired shaft furnaces gave argentiferous lead, most commonly about 2,000 g of silver to a tonne of lead; cupellation under blown air then oxidised the lead to litharge (lead oxide) and left the silver.
note: In F. Hulek, H. Lohmann, S. Nomicos and A. Hauptmann (eds), Laurion. Interdisciplinary Approaches to an Ancient Greek Mining Landscape (Deutsches Bergbau-Museum Bochum, 2023), pp. 87–104; open access. The author, of the School of Mining and Metallurgy at the National Technical University of Athens, gives the smelting charge as mainly cerussite with galena up to about 20 per cent, and silver contents of 1,000–4,000 g a tonne depending on the ore. A technical account across periods; it does not trace the silver of any particular coin.
